The risk to LPKF is less competitive displacement than secular volume attrition: an installed base that renews slowly, with new unit sales dependent on the formation of new R&D programmes rather than replacement cycles.

## Glass Substrates: The Open Field

The competitive terrain shifts entirely when LPKF's LIDE technology is considered. LIDE — Laser Induced Deep Etching — is a two-step process in which ultrafast laser pulses create damage tracks through glass at high aspect ratios, which are then developed by wet chemical etch into precision through-glass vias (TGVs) and patterned features. The technology is aimed at the emerging glass-core substrate market for semiconductor advanced packaging, where the industry is exploring glass as an alternative to the organic laminates that have served as the foundation of high-density interconnect packages for two decades.

Intel's September 2023 glass-substrate disclosure functioned as the clearest public market-formation signal for the entire supply chain. Intel said it was on track to deliver complete glass-substrate solutions in the second half of the decade because glass offered flatter surfaces, better thermal and mechanical stability and the potential for far denser interconnect design rules than organic substrates. The trade-offs remained real — brittleness, new process integration requirements and the capital cost of converting packaging lines — but the market direction was no longer hypothetical. [Intel Newsroom](<https://newsroom.intel.com/artificial-intelligence/intel-unveils-industry-leading-glass-substrates>)

The competitive set in glass processing was therefore heterogeneous rather than a tidy list of direct substitutes. Hamamatsu's official positioning around Stealth Dicing emphasized a completely dry laser-dicing process with no kerf loss, no chipping and high bending strength — clearly relevant to brittle-material processing, but not the same process flow as LPKF's laser-plus-wet-etch TGV route. LPKF's own LIDE materials, by contrast, emphasized 5 µm minimum feature sizes, aspect ratios up to 1:50 and panel-level processing on 515 mm × 510 mm substrates. [Hamamatsu Stealth Dicing](<https://www.hamamatsu.com/us/en/product/semiconductor-manufacturing-support-systems/stealth-dicing-technology.html>), [LIDE technology](<https://lide.lpkf.com/en/technology/lide>), [NEXAR LIDE systems](<https://lide.lpkf.com/en/systems/nexar-lide>)

Vitrion also needed a factual reset here. It was not publicly framed as an outside substrate manufacturer or joint venture taking LIDE off LPKF's hands; the Vitrion site described it as a brand of LPKF and a foundry service. That still implied a commercialization model broader than one-off machine sales, but it kept the execution risk squarely on LPKF's own balance sheet and operating capabilities. [Vitrion company](<https://vitrion.lpkf.com/en/company>)

| Company / process | Officially advertised focus before 23 May 2026 | Read-through for LPKF |
|---|---|---|
| LPKF LIDE | 5 µm minimum feature size, 1:50 aspect ratio, up to 515 mm × 510 mm panels | Direct TGV and glass-core-substrate platform |
| Hamamatsu Stealth Dicing | Dry brittle-material wafer dicing with no kerf loss or chipping | Adjacent brittle-material laser processing, not a wet-etch TGV flow |
| 3D-Micromac | PV, semiconductor, display-and-smart-glass and wafer processing | Adjacent glass and wafer micromachining exposure |
| LASEA | Ultrafast laser micromachining across medtech, electronics, semiconductors and luxury | Adjacent ultrafast-laser precision peer |

The competitive position LPKF held going into 2026 was, in sum, one of differentiated technology awaiting commercial validation. In laser micromachining and PCB prototyping, its moats were real but sized to markets that did not excite large-scale competitors. In glass substrates, it had arrived early at what might yet prove to be a significant inflection in semiconductor packaging — carrying proprietary process IP and an in-house foundry-and-service route to scaling, but facing a validation timeline that had consistently slipped to the right across the industry.

chapters.title: Timeline from 1976 through LIDE positioning
chapters.body:
## The Founding Arc

LPKF dated its foundation to 4 August 1976 and said engineer Juergen Seebach developed its first mechanical PCB-production process. That origin mattered because the company kept returning to the same commercial logic: compress engineering cycle times, then widen the toolset around that speed advantage. [LPKF company profile](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/company/company-profile>)

## The Laser Tool Milestones

The chronology on the company profile marked 1989 as the year LPKF developed laser-based PCB structuring, 1993 as the debut of the first StencilLaser system and 1998 as the IPO. A later ProtoLaser retrospective added the next level of detail, saying the first commercial ProtoLaser reached the market in 2000 after beginning as a 1989 research project with the University of Hannover. [LPKF company profile](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/company/company-profile>), [25 Years ProtoLaser](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/25-years-protolaser-from-vision-to-precision-revolution-in-electronics-manufacturing>)

In parallel, the company profile placed the start of laser plastic welding in 2000, when LPKF said it joined forces with a specialist team from the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg and opened new markets such as automotive. In 2006, the chronology said LPKF's LDS process entered high-volume antenna manufacturing, creating the basis for the handset-era Electronics franchise. [LPKF company profile](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/company/company-profile>)

## Solar, Glass and the New Optionality

LPKF entered the photovoltaic market in 2007 through thin-film module structuring systems in Suhl. Much later, in 2017, the company won Productronica's Innovation Award for LIDE and its Vitrion 5000 system, making glass processing a visible part of the corporate story. The company profile then marked 2019 as the opening of the Vitrion Foundry in Garbsen for display and semiconductor customers. [LPKF company profile](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/company/company-profile>), [LPKF LIDE award, 2017](<https://www.lpkf.com/fileadmin/mediafiles/user_upload/news-and-press/press-downloads/2017/4341-pr-lpkf-wins-productronica-innovation-award-2017.pdf>)

By September 2024, management had shifted from technology evangelism to ecosystem-building. LPKF said it was creating a glass-focused supply chain for advanced packaging and could support customers either by integrating LIDE into their process flow or by offering small- to high-volume manufacturing through the Vitrion foundry. That language was a more concrete commercialization step than the earlier generic IR framing. [LPKF partner network](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-builds-partner-network-to-innovate-glass-substrate-production-for-semiconductor-packaging>)

## The 2024-2026 Sequence

Three events then made the LIDE story materially more tangible. First, on 13 December 2024, LPKF disclosed its first purchase agreement for several LIDE systems for series production of display applications, in the mid seven-digit euro range. Second, in April 2025, LPKF and Onto Innovation said Onto's Firefly inspection system would be installed in the Vitrion cleanroom in Hanover to support high-throughput quality control of glass substrates and interposers. Third, in October 2025, LPKF said it had become one of the initiators of Fraunhofer IZM's 15-company Glass Panel Technology Group, launched on 1 October 2025 to industrialize glass-panel process chains such as TGV and RDL. [EQS ad-hoc, 13 December 2024](https://www.eqs-news.com/news/ad-hoc/lpkf-receives-order-for-series-production-with-lide-in-the-display-sector/b13f7624-08db-406d-af36-35ae5962c4c2_en), [Onto Innovation / LPKF](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/onto-innovation-and-lpkf-are-set-to-accelerate-mass-production-of-glass-core-substrates-for-semiconductors>), [Fraunhofer GPTG](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-delivers-key-strategic-technology-to-fraunhofers-glass-panel-technology-group>)

Running alongside that technology cadence was a worsening earnings cadence. LPKF cut 2024 guidance in October and again in December, then reported 2024 revenue of €122.9 million and EBIT of –€2.5 million. On 15 September 2025 it launched North Star, the multi-year restructuring programme aimed at a sustainable double-digit EBIT margin by 2028. Full-year 2025 revenue then fell to €115.3 million, reported EBIT to –€13.5 million, and order backlog to €27.0 million. [LPKF nine-month 2024 report](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-se-business-performance-after-nine-months-of-2024>), [EQS ad-hoc, 9 December 2024](<https://www.eqs-news.com/news/ad-hoc/lpkf-senkt-die-umsatz-und-ergebnisprognose-fur-das-gesamtjahr-2024/cd66d3c3-cdb7-456d-8add-d9058c1b7df6_en>), [LPKF annual report 2025](<https://www.lpkf.com/fileadmin/mediafiles/user_upload/company/investor-relations/financial-reports/2025/LPKF_Annual_Report_2025.pdf>), [North Star programme](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-strengthens-structural-resilience-north-star-initiative-aims-to-secure-long-term-profitability>)

## The Near-Term Catalyst Window

By the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026, the key catalyst window had narrowed into something more precise than the old draft's generalized optimism. The company had a first display-production order, a foundry-and-metrology setup in Hanover, a role in a Fraunhofer-led glass-panel consortium and explicit statements that numerous semiconductor customers were using LIDE in test and R&D environments. What it still lacked was disclosed high-volume advanced-packaging revenue. Management's own 2026 guidance excluded any such orders because downstream qualification steps remained the pacing item. [LPKF Q1 2026 release](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-gets-off-to-a-solid-start-in-2026>), [LPKF Q1 2026 report](<https://www.lpkf.com/fileadmin/mediafiles/user_upload/company/investor-relations/financial-reports/2026/LPKF_Quarterly_Financial_Report_Q1_2026.pdf>)

Taken together, the news flow had become more binary than the earlier version of this dossier admitted. The company had moved well beyond a laboratory thesis, but it had not yet crossed into repeatable semiconductor volume. That was the inflection window investors were really watching.

chapters.title: LIDE IP, laser micromachining IP, patent portfolio
chapters.body:
## The Architecture of a Laser IP Estate

LPKF accumulated a proprietary technology catalogue through decades of incremental innovation, where each product generation funded the next layer of intellectual property. By the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, that estate rested on two distinct but reinforcing pillars — the mature licensing engine of Laser Direct Structuring and the emerging, strategically critical claims staked around Laser Induced Deep Etching (LIDE) for glass substrates.

## LIDE: Filing Around a Process, Not Just a Machine

LIDE's patent architecture reflects how LPKF approached the glass processing opportunity: not merely as a capital equipment provider selling a tool, but as the inventor of a method that controls the full process chain. The core LIDE mechanism couples an ultrashort-pulse (USP) laser — operating in the picosecond to femtosecond range — with a selective wet-chemical etch, typically hydrofluoric acid chemistry. The laser modifies the glass lattice along precisely defined filament paths without ablating material outright; the subsequent etch then attacks only the modified zones, leaving surrounding glass structurally intact. The combination produces through-holes and cavities with aspect ratios exceeding 20:1, tolerances measured in single-digit micrometres, and smooth sidewalls unsuitable for competing techniques including mechanical micro-drilling or standard CO₂ ablation.

The IP scope accordingly covers both the laser parameter space — pulse duration, repetition rate, focal geometry and beam shaping — and the process chemistry that determines etch selectivity. LPKF's current LIDE materials said the process could deliver via diameters down to 5 µm, aspect ratios up to 1:50 and sidewall roughness below Ra 0.1 µm, which helps explain why the company kept extending the patent estate into throughput and process-control questions rather than only machine architecture. On 2 September 2025, LPKF also said additional Korean patent protection effective 1 September 2025 covered the characteristic "earthworm structure" formed in processed TGVs. [LIDE technology](<https://lide.lpkf.com/en/technology/lide>), [NEXAR LIDE systems](<https://lide.lpkf.com/en/systems/nexar-lide>), [Korea patent release](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-strengthens-lide-technology-leadership-with-new-patent-protection-in-korea>)

Vitrion, meanwhile, was not publicly presented as a joint venture. The current site described it as a brand of LPKF and as a specialized foundry service, which meant the manufacturing know-how and commercialization overlay around LIDE remained visibly inside the group rather than being parked in a separately disclosed vehicle. [Vitrion company](<https://vitrion.lpkf.com/en/company>)

## LDS: A Licensing Model That Proved the Template

Laser Direct Structuring supplied the proof of concept that LIDE investors and observers examined most carefully. LPKF had pioneered LDS — the two-stage process of laser-activating a proprietary additive embedded in injection-moulded polymer, then selectively metallising the activated zones — in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Patent protection on the core LDS method, the laser-activatable material chemistry (developed in collaboration with material partners), and the metallisation sequence built a licensing estate that generated recurring royalty income from every LDS-equipped production line installed outside LPKF's own equipment sales.

The LDS licensing model demonstrated that LPKF could extract value beyond equipment hardware, collecting per-part or per-run royalties as the antenna and sensor applications built on LDS technology scaled into hundreds of millions of units annually in consumer electronics. That revenue stream buffered cyclical swings in equipment demand and validated the company's approach of building IP rather than settling for process-equipment supplier status. When LIDE's semiconductor packaging opportunity began attracting serious industry attention through 2023–2025, management pointed to LDS licensing's margin profile as the appropriate financial analogy for what a mature LIDE position might eventually generate.

## The Broader Laser Micromachining Estate

Beyond LIDE and LDS, LPKF's filed portfolio reached across its four operating segments. Laser plastic welding — the Welding segment's core — carried claims around contour and quasi-simultaneous welding geometries, along with the optical delivery systems that enable through-transmission joining at the tolerances automotive and medical device customers demand. PCB prototyping and rapid-routing tools, commercialised since the 1990s, were protected by claims on laser parameter selection for dielectric materials, mechanical handling integration, and the software-controlled process sequencing that competitors reverse-engineering the hardware could not trivially reproduce.

The cumulative result was a portfolio spanning materials types — glass, polymer, semiconductor, metallic interconnect layers — and wavelength regimes from UV excimer to near-IR solid-state to the ultrashort-pulse domain. Breadth of that kind is defensively useful: a customer evaluating LPKF against a specialist rival in any single application confronted not just a machine comparison but a licensing exposure question.

## R&D Organisation and Investment Discipline

LPKF maintained its primary R&D operations at the Garbsen headquarters campus outside Hannover, where process development, systems engineering and applications laboratories shared physical proximity. A US technology centre in Wilsonville, Oregon, served the North American semiconductor and electronics customer base and provided an outpost for engaging with advanced packaging ecosystem partners operating on Pacific time.

Collaboration with Fraunhofer institutes, particularly in optics and photonics, gave LPKF access to applied-research capacity without carrying the full cost of basic science infrastructure. Joint development agreements structured with such partners typically allowed LPKF to retain exclusive commercial licensing rights to resulting IP, a model common among well-managed German Mittelstand technology companies with histories of successful academic technology transfer.

R&D investment across the restructuring years of 2023 and 2024 remained elevated relative to revenue as the company deliberately funded LIDE process refinement and the engineering work required to bring glass substrate processing to the panel dimensions advanced packaging customers specified. That decision — to protect the technology investment cycle even as topline revenue contracted — reflected management's calculation that the LIDE window of competitive advantage was finite and front-loading the patent estate would determine whether LPKF entered the glass substrate era as a licensor or merely a toll-road equipment vendor. The distinction carried substantial long-run margin implications for every scenario in which glass core substrates achieved material penetration in AI and high-performance computing packaging stacks.

chapters.title: LIDE commercial uncertainty, segment cyclicality, FX, competitive, governance, scale
chapters.body:
## The Spectrum of Structural Risk

For a company whose equity story rests on a technology that has not yet generated material revenue, the principal risk sits squarely in the gap between proof of concept and commercial scale. LPKF's balance sheet was strained by the restructuring actions of 2023 and 2024. The combination of execution risk in LIDE glass processing, cyclicality in the legacy segments, foreign-exchange translation drag, intensifying competition, thin governance protections, and capital scarcity creates a layered risk profile that investors must disaggregate before assigning probability weights to the bull case.

---

## LIDE: The Inflection Clock

The most consequential uncertainty through the 2026–2028 window was the timing of commercial inflection for LIDE. The technology promised a pathway into glass core substrates for semiconductor advanced packaging — a segment analysts at SEMI and Yole Développement identified as structurally durable. The hyperscale compute buildout was adding urgency to the packaging transition.

The problem for LPKF was sequencing. The company had invested in LIDE development and was trying to commercialize it through its own Vitrion foundry-and-service model, but as of 23 May 2026 the disclosed record still showed a technology in qualification rather than one already earning repeatable semiconductor volume. The capital cycle in advanced packaging is long: LPKF itself said the timing of any high-volume ramp depended on downstream qualification steps, which is why such orders were excluded from 2026 guidance. Each quarter of delay extended the period during which the company was effectively funding LIDE through cash generated by slower-growth legacy segments. [LPKF annual report 2025](<https://www.lpkf.com/fileadmin/mediafiles/user_upload/company/investor-relations/financial-reports/2025/LPKF_Annual_Report_2025.pdf>), [LPKF Q1 2026 release](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-gets-off-to-a-solid-start-in-2026>), [Vitrion company](<https://vitrion.lpkf.com/en/company>)

---

## Segment Cyclicality

Each segment carried cyclical exposure. Development was tightly correlated with electronics R&D investment cycles — capital expenditure on prototyping equipment is discretionary in ways that production tooling is not. Electronics and Welding both carried meaningful automotive end-market exposure; a sustained automotive downturn hit two of four segments simultaneously. Solar faced persistent margin compression as Chinese equipment producers moved up the value chain.

---

## Foreign Exchange and EUR Translation

LPKF reported in euros and generated the majority of its corporate costs in euros, but its customer base was genuinely global — spanning European electronics manufacturers, North American PCB prototyping shops, and increasingly Asian semiconductor packaging customers. Revenue booked in US dollars, South Korean won, Japanese yen, or Chinese renminbi all translated back to euros at prevailing exchange rates, and the euro's trajectory against the dollar through 2024 and into 2025 had been volatile enough to introduce meaningful translation noise into reported figures. A one-cent move in the EUR/USD rate against a comparable prior-period average could shift reported revenue by several hundred thousand euros on a base of this scale, and hedging capacity at LPKF's size was structurally limited relative to a large-cap industrial exporter with dedicated treasury operations. The FX overlay was particularly relevant for LIDE revenue if and when it arrived: semiconductor packaging customers in Taiwan and South Korea would almost certainly negotiate contracts denominated in US dollars or local currency, adding translation exposure at precisely the moment LPKF would most need clean revenue comparisons to validate the technology story to Frankfurt equity investors.

---

## Competitive Intensity

LPKF occupied a defensible niche in laser micromachining but it was not uncontested. In PCB prototyping, the company held a market-leading position built over decades, but competitors including LPKF's historical German peers and several Asian systems integrators continued to attack the segment on price. In glass processing — the forward growth arena — the competitive horizon was wider and the incumbents more formidable. Corning's internal processing capabilities, partnerships involving Coherent's ultrashort-pulse laser platforms, and emerging work from Asian laser OEMs targeting the same advanced-packaging glass market all represented credible threats. LASEA, the Belgian precision laser specialist, competed in overlapping ultrafast-laser micromachining applications. The distinguishing claim for LIDE was its specific process window for through-glass via formation and panel-level scribing, but intellectual property in laser micromachining is susceptible to design-around, and a well-capitalised competitor with deep application engineering resources could close the gap faster than the LPKF balance sheet could maintain a development lead.

---

## Governance and SDAX Small-Cap Status

LPKF's liquidity and coverage profile remained that of a Frankfurt small cap even after STOXX removed the shares from the SDAX in December 2025. The company still operated under Germany's two-tier supervisory-board structure, but the market context was the more important point: modest trading liquidity, thinner sell-side coverage and a technology story that required patience made the valuation unusually sensitive to sentiment swings around semiconductor packaging. [Deutsche Börse, 4 December 2025](<https://live.deutsche-boerse.com/news/selection-indices-aumovio-and-tkms-will-be-included-in-mdax>), [LPKF management](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/company/management>)

---

## Scale and Capital Constraints

The synthesis of the above risks converged on a single structural constraint: size. LPKF still had only €115.3 million of revenue in 2025 and a backlog of €27.0 million at year-end, even though it had extended its syndicated financing through 31 December 2028. That was enough runway to keep investing, but not enough to make execution errors cheap. The path through the inflection still required the company to remain solvent and credible long enough for LIDE adoption to accelerate — a window that, in semiconductor-capital-equipment cycles, is usually measured in years rather than quarters. chapters.title: LIDE inflection, core segment recovery, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The geometry of a bet

By spring 2026, LPKF had emerged from two years of restructuring as a leaner operation. The machinery was running again. The question the market was pricing was whether LPKF had timed the arrival of its strategic optionality correctly — whether LIDE, commercialized through LPKF's own branded Vitrion foundry-and-service model, would reach commercial inflection during the semiconductor industry's search for advanced packaging substrates.

## Glass substrates and the packaging inflection

Organic laminates were beginning to hit physical limits relevant to the chiplet era. Intel's September 2023 glass-substrate announcement was the clearest public statement of the industry's direction: it said glass offered flatter surfaces, better thermal and mechanical stability and an order-of-magnitude improvement in the design rules needed for future data-center and AI products, with delivery targeted for the second half of the decade. LPKF's own LIDE materials positioned the company for precisely that gap, advertising 5 µm minimum feature sizes and aspect ratios up to 1:50 in glass. Whether the industry would adopt glass broadly on a timetable that matched LPKF's commercial planning horizon remained open, but the directional case was no longer just theoretical. [Intel Newsroom](<https://newsroom.intel.com/artificial-intelligence/intel-unveils-industry-leading-glass-substrates>), [LIDE technology](<https://lide.lpkf.com/en/technology/lide>), [NEXAR LIDE systems](<https://lide.lpkf.com/en/systems/nexar-lide>)

For a company of LPKF's size, the asymmetry was notable. A glass substrate tooling market that achieved even a fraction of the scale that organic substrate tooling had reached would represent a revenue opportunity many times the company's then-current turnover. The risk, symmetrically, was that the transition would prove slower, more technically contested, or more dominated by incumbent equipment makers than the LIDE framing assumed.

## Vitrion and the commercialisation structure

The vehicle LPKF used to bring LIDE to market was Vitrion, but the factual record differed from the draft's partnership framing. Vitrion described itself as a brand of LPKF and a specialized foundry service. By the frozen window, the public record around it had become fuller than the draft suggested: Onto's Firefly tool was due into the Vitrion cleanroom in Hanover, LPKF had publicly positioned the foundry as a route from sampling to small- and high-volume glass-core manufacturing, and the Vitrion site publicly named Dr. Rafael Santos and Dr.-Ing. Maik Bertke as operating contacts. What still had not appeared was disclosed semiconductor volume revenue or named production customers. [Vitrion company](<https://vitrion.lpkf.com/en/company>), [Onto Innovation / LPKF](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/onto-innovation-and-lpkf-are-set-to-accelerate-mass-production-of-glass-core-substrates-for-semiconductors>), [LPKF partner network](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-builds-partner-network-to-innovate-glass-substrate-production-for-semiconductor-packaging>)

## Core segments: the floor under the option

The optionality framing was sustainable only if the core business provided a stable earnings base. Here the post-restructuring picture was more legible, if not uniformly encouraging.

The Development segment — PCB prototyping systems sold to electronics manufacturers, research institutions, and engineering teams that needed rapid-iteration circuit boards — had long been LPKF's most durable franchise. The company's prototyping equipment occupied a near-monopoly position in several sub-niches; no serious competitor had dislodged it at the precision end of the market. Volume was modest and the growth ceiling was limited by the size of the addressable prototyping population, but the revenue was recurring in character and not heavily cyclical.

The Electronics segment, which housed both SMT tools and LIDE, remained exposed to discretionary capital spending, but the recovery signal was more modest than the old draft implied. Segment revenue slipped slightly to €35.9 million in 2025 from €36.9 million in 2024. The encouraging sign arrived in orders rather than reported sales: management said Q1 2026 order intake improved significantly, especially for PCB depaneling systems, suggesting that some of the earlier investment paralysis was easing even though the segment had not yet put up a decisive revenue rebound. [LPKF annual report 2025](<https://www.lpkf.com/fileadmin/mediafiles/user_upload/company/investor-relations/financial-reports/2025/LPKF_Annual_Report_2025.pdf>), [LPKF Q1 2026 release](<https://www.lpkf.com/en/news-press/press-releases-teaser/lpkf-gets-off-to-a-solid-start-in-2026>)

The Solar segment, which provided laser processing equipment for cell manufacturers, sat in a more complicated position. European solar manufacturing had not recovered the strategic momentum that policymakers had periodically promised it, and the Chinese dominance of cell production capacity had continued to concentrate purchasing decisions in a geography where LPKF's pricing position was under persistent pressure. The segment was not viewed as a core growth driver for the 2026-2030 horizon.

Welding — laser plastic welding systems sold primarily to automotive and medical device manufacturers — provided a steadier contribution. The automotive transition toward electrification had created mixed signals: some traditional plastic assembly applications declined as vehicle architectures changed, but EV battery housings and power electronics enclosures introduced new welding opportunities at different material specifications. The segment was not expected to generate headline growth, but its margin profile was defensible.

## The 2026-2030 posture

The strategic posture LPKF carried into the second half of the 2020s could be read as a two-phase construction. Phase one was the consolidation already underway: operating expenditure discipline, segment focus, and the gradual recovery of Electronics and Welding demand as the 2023-2024 downturn cycled through. Phase two — the one that justified the multiple the market was assigning to the equity — was contingent on LIDE and Vitrion converting the glass substrate thesis into disclosed customer engagements and, eventually, recurring system sales.

The timing uncertainty around phase two was the central analytical variable. Glass substrate adoption at volume required not only that chipmakers choose glass over organic, but that their foundry and OSAT partners invest in the tooling and process qualification at scale — a decision with a multi-year capital commitment horizon. If the industry moved toward glass substrates in the 2027-2028 window, LPKF and Vitrion would be positioned to participate in the early equipment orders. If the transition stalled at pilot-line volumes through the end of the decade, the company would need the core segments to carry more of the earnings burden than the current trajectory comfortably supported.

What LPKF had assembled by the May 2026 snapshot was a business that had survived its restructuring with its principal technologies intact, had packaged its most consequential strategic bet into a branded foundry-and-systems offering that semiconductor customers could engage with seriously, and had retained enough financing flexibility to keep funding development. The 2026-2030 question was therefore not whether the glass opportunity was technically real. It was whether a roughly €115 million-revenue German laser-systems specialist could translate that position into disclosed, repeatable volume before the patience demanded by North Star and the advanced-packaging qualification cycle ran out.
